subject: biology
specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology guide, first assessment 2025

statements.understanding: Water as the medium for life
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that the first cells originated in water and that water remains the medium in which most processes of life occur.

statements.understanding: Hydrogen bonds as a consequence of the polar covalent bonds within water molecules
statements.guidance: Students should understand that polarity of covalent bonding within water molecules is due to unequal sharing of electrons and that hydrogen bonding due to this polarity occurs between water molecules. Students should be able to represent two or more water molecules and hydrogen bonds between them with the notation shown below to indicate polarity.

statements.understanding: Cohesion of water molecules due to hydrogen bonding and consequences for organisms
statements.guidance: Include transport of water under tension in xylem and the use of water surfaces as habitats due to the effect known as surface tension.

statements.understanding: Adhesion of water to materials that are polar or charged and impacts for organisms
statements.guidance: Include capillary action in soil and in plant cell walls.

statements.understanding: Solvent properties of water linked to its role as a medium for metabolism and for transport in
statements.guidance: plants and animals Emphasize that a wide variety of hydrophilic molecules dissolve in water and that most enzymes catalyse reactions in aqueous solution. Students should also understand that the functions of some molecules in cells depend on them being hydrophobic and insoluble.

statements.understanding: Physical properties of water and the consequences for animals in aquatic habitats
statements.guidance: Include buoyancy, viscosity, thermal conductivity and specific heat capacity. Contrast the physical properties of water with those of air and illustrate the consequences using examples of animals that live in water and in air or on land, such as the black-throated loon (Gavia arctica) and the ringed seal (Pusa hispida). Note: When students are referring to an organism in an examination, either the common name or the scientific name is acceptable.

statements.understanding: Extraplanetary origin of water on Earth and reasons for its retention
statements.guidance: The abundance of water over billions of years of Earth’s history has allowed life to evolve. Limit hypotheses for the origin of water on Earth to asteroids and reasons for retention to gravity and temperatures low enough to condense water.

statements.understanding: Relationship between the search for extraterrestrial life and the presence of water
statements.guidance: Include the idea of the “Goldilocks zone”.

statements.understanding: DNA as the genetic material of all living organisms
statements.guidance: Some viruses use RNA as their genetic material but viruses are not considered to be living.

statements.understanding: Components of a nucleotide
statements.guidance: In diagrams of nucleotides use circles, pentagons and rectangles to represent relative positions of phosphates, pentose sugars and bases.

statements.understanding: Sugar–phosphate bonding and the sugar–phosphate “backbone” of DNA and RNA
statements.guidance: Sugar–phosphate bonding makes a continuous chain of covalently bonded atoms in each strand of DNA or RNA nucleotides, which forms a strong “backbone” in the molecule.

statements.understanding: Bases in each nucleic acid that form the basis of a code
statements.guidance: Students should know the names of the nitrogenous bases.

statements.understanding: RNA as a polymer formed by condensation of nucleotide monomers
statements.guidance: Students should be able to draw and recognize diagrams of the structure of single nucleotides and RNA polymers.

statements.understanding: DNA as a double helix made of two antiparallel strands of nucleotides with two strands linked by
statements.guidance: hydrogen bonding between complementary base pairs In diagrams of DNA structure, students should draw the two strands antiparallel, but are not required to draw the helical shape. Students should show adenine (A) paired with thymine (T), and guanine (G) paired with cytosine (C). Students are not required to memorize the relative lengths of the purine and pyrimidine bases, or the numbers of hydrogen bonds.

statements.understanding: Differences between DNA and RNA
statements.guidance: Include the number of strands present, the types of nitrogenous bases and the type of pentose sugar. Students should be able to sketch the difference between ribose and deoxyribose. Students should be familiar with examples of nucleic acids.

statements.understanding: Role of complementary base pairing in allowing genetic information to be replicated and
statements.guidance: expressed Students should understand that complementarity is based on hydrogen bonding.

statements.understanding: Diversity of possible DNA base sequences and the limitless capacity of DNA for storing
statements.guidance: information Explain that diversity by any length of DNA molecule and any base sequence is possible. Emphasize the enormous capacity of DNA for storing data with great economy.

statements.understanding: Conservation of the genetic code across all life forms as evidence of universal common ancestry
statements.guidance: Students are not required to memorize any specific examples.

statements.understanding: Directionality of RNA and DNA
statements.guidance: Include 5' to 3' linkages in the sugar–phosphate backbone and their significance for replication, transcription and translation.

statements.understanding: Purine-to-pyrimidine bonding as a component of DNA helix stability
statements.guidance: Adenine–thymine (A–T) and cytosine–guanine (C–G) pairs have equal length, so the DNA helix has the same three-dimensional structure, regardless of the base sequence.

statements.understanding: Structure of a nucleosome
statements.guidance: Limit to a DNA molecule wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins held together by an additional histone protein attached to linker DNA. Application of skills: Students are required to use molecular visualization software to study the association between the proteins and DNA within a nucleosome.

statements.understanding: Evidence from the Hershey–Chase experiment for DNA as the genetic material
statements.guidance: Students should understand how the results of the experiment support the conclusion that DNA is the genetic material. NOS: Students should appreciate that technological developments can open up new possibilities for experiments. When radioisotopes were made available to scientists as research tools, the Hershey–Chase experiment became possible.

statements.understanding: Chargaff’s data on the relative amounts of pyrimidine and purine bases across diverse life forms
statements.guidance: NOS: Students should understand how the “problem of induction” is addressed by the “certainty of falsification”. In this case, Chargaff’s data falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis that there was a repeating sequence of the four bases in DNA.

statements.understanding: Conditions on early Earth and the pre-biotic formation of carbon compounds
statements.guidance: Include the lack of free oxygen and therefore ozone, higher concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane, resulting in higher temperatures and ultraviolet light penetration. The conditions may have caused a variety of carbon compounds to form spontaneously by chemical processes that do not now occur.

statements.understanding: Cells as the smallest units of self-sustaining life
statements.guidance: Discuss the differences between something that is living and something that is non-living. Include reasons that viruses are considered to be non-living.

statements.understanding: Challenge of explaining the spontaneous origin of cells
statements.guidance: Cells are highly complex structures that can currently only be produced by division of pre-existing cells. Students should be aware that catalysis, self-replication of molecules, self-assembly and the emergence of compartmentalization were necessary requirements for the evolution of the first cells. NOS: Students should appreciate that claims in science, including hypotheses and theories, must be testable. In some cases, scientists have to struggle with hypotheses that are difficult to test. In this case the exact conditions on pre-biotic Earth cannot be replicated and the first protocells did not fossilize.

statements.understanding: Evidence for the origin of carbon compounds
statements.guidance: Evaluate the Miller–Urey experiment.

statements.understanding: Spontaneous formation of vesicles by coalescence of fatty acids into spherical bilayers
statements.guidance: Formation of a membrane-bound compartment is needed to allow internal chemistry to become different from that outside the compartment.

statements.understanding: RNA as a presumed first genetic material
statements.guidance: RNA can be replicated and has some catalytic activity so it may have acted initially as both the genetic material and the enzymes of the earliest cells. Ribozymes in the ribosome are still used to catalyse peptide bond formation during protein synthesis.

statements.understanding: Evidence for a last universal common ancestor
statements.guidance: Include the universal genetic code and shared genes across all organisms. Include the likelihood of other forms of life having evolved but becoming extinct due to competition from the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) and descendants of LUCA.

statements.understanding: Approaches used to estimate dates of the first living cells and the last universal common ancestor
statements.guidance: Students should develop an appreciation of the immense length of time over which life has been evolving on Earth.

statements.understanding: Evidence for the evolution of the last universal common ancestor in the vicinity of hydrothermal
statements.guidance: vents Include fossilized evidence of life from ancient seafloor hydrothermal vent precipitates and evidence of conserved sequences from genomic analysis.

statements.understanding: Cells as the basic structural unit of all living organisms
statements.guidance: NOS: Students should be aware that deductive reason can be used to generate predictions from theories. Based on cell theory, a newly discovered organism can be predicted to consist of one or more cells.

statements.understanding: Microscopy skills
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should have experience of making temporary mounts of cells and tissues, staining, measuring sizes using an eyepiece graticule, focusing with coarse and fine adjustments, calculating actual size and magnification, producing a scale bar and taking photographs. NOS: Students should appreciate that measurement using instruments is a form of quantitative observation.

statements.understanding: Developments in microscopy
statements.guidance: Include the advantages of electron microscopy, freeze fracture, cryogenic electron microscopy, and the use of fluorescent stains and immunofluorescence in light microscopy.

statements.understanding: Structures common to cells in all living organisms
statements.guidance: Typical cells have DNA as genetic material and a cytoplasm composed mainly of water, which is enclosed by a plasma membrane composed of lipids. Students should understand the reasons for these structures.

statements.understanding: Prokaryote cell structure
statements.guidance: Include these cell components: cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop and 70S ribosomes. The type of prokaryotic cell structure required is that of Gram-positive eubacteria such as Bacillus and Staphylococcus. Students should appreciate that prokaryote cell structure varies. However, students are not required to know details of the variations such as the lack of cell walls in phytoplasmas and mycoplasmas.

statements.understanding: Eukaryote cell structure
statements.guidance: Students should be familiar with features common to eukaryote cells: a plasma membrane enclosing a compartmentalized cytoplasm with 80S ribosomes; a nucleus with chromosomes made of DNA bound to histones, contained in a double membrane with pores; membrane-bound cytoplasmic organelles including mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and a variety of vesicles or vacuoles including lysosomes; and a cytoskeleton of microtubules and microfilaments.

statements.understanding: Processes of life in unicellular organisms
statements.guidance: Include these functions: homeostasis, metabolism, nutrition, movement, excretion, growth, response to stimuli and reproduction.

statements.understanding: Differences in eukaryotic cell structure between animals, fungi and plants
statements.guidance: Include presence and composition of cell walls, differences in size and function of vacuoles, presence of chloroplasts and other plastids, and presence of centrioles, cilia and flagella.

statements.understanding: Atypical cell structure in eukaryotes
statements.guidance: Use numbers of nuclei to illustrate one type of atypical cell structure in aseptate fungal hyphae, skeletal muscle, red blood cells and phloem sieve tube elements.

statements.understanding: Cell types and cell structures viewed in light and electron micrographs
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should be able to identify cells in light and electron micrographs as prokaryote, plant or animal. In electron micrographs, students should be able to identify these structures: nucleoid region, prokaryotic cell wall, nucleus, mitochondrion, chloroplast, sap vacuole, Golgi apparatus, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, chromosomes, ribosomes, cell wall, plasma membrane and microvilli.

statements.understanding: Drawing and annotation based on electron micrographs
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should be able to draw and annotate diagrams of organelles (nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, sap vacuole, Golgi apparatus, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum and chromosomes) as well as other cell structures (cell wall, plasma membrane, secretory vesicles and microvilli) shown in electron micrographs. Students are required to include the functions in their annotations.

statements.understanding: Origin of eukaryotic cells by endosymbiosis
statements.guidance: Evidence suggests that all eukaryotes evolved from a common unicellular ancestor that had a nucleus and reproduced sexually. Mitochondria then evolved by endosymbiosis. In some eukaryotes, chloroplasts subsequently also had an endosymbiotic origin. Evidence should include the presence in mitochondria and chloroplasts of 70S ribosomes, naked circular DNA and the ability to replicate. NOS: Students should recognize that the strength of a theory comes from the observations the theory explains and the predictions it supports. A wide range of observations are accounted for by the theory of endosymbiosis.

statements.understanding: Cell differentiation as the process for developing specialized tissues in multicellular organisms
statements.guidance: Students should be aware that the basis for differentiation is different patterns of gene expression often triggered by changes in the environment.

statements.understanding: Evolution of multicellularity
statements.guidance: Students should be aware that multicellularity has evolved repeatedly. Many fungi and eukaryotic algae and all plants and animals are multicellular. Multicellularity has the advantages of allowing larger body size and cell specialization.

statements.understanding: Structural features common to viruses
statements.guidance: Relatively few features are shared by all viruses: small, fixed size; nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes.

statements.understanding: Diversity of structure in viruses
statements.guidance: Students should understand that viruses are highly diverse in their shape and structure. Genetic material may be RNA or DNA, which can be either single- or double-stranded. Some viruses are enveloped in host cell membrane and others are not enveloped. Virus examples include bacteriophage lambda, coronaviruses and HIV.

statements.understanding: Lytic cycle of a virus
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that viruses rely on a host cell for energy supply, nutrition, protein synthesis and other life functions. Use bacteriophage lambda as an example of the phases in a lytic cycle. A.2.3.4—Lysogenic cycle of a virus Use bacteriophage lambda as an example.

statements.understanding: Evidence for several origins of viruses from other organisms
statements.guidance: The diversity of viruses suggests several possible origins. Viruses share an extreme form of obligate parasitism as a mode of existence, so the structural features that they have in common could be regarded as convergent evolution. The genetic code is shared between viruses and living organisms.

statements.understanding: Rapid evolution in viruses
statements.guidance: Include reasons for very rapid rates of evolution in some viruses. Use two examples of rapid evolution: evolution of influenza viruses and of HIV. Consider the consequences for treating diseases caused by rapidly evolving viruses.

statements.understanding: Variation between organisms as a defining feature of life
statements.guidance: Students should understand that no two individuals are identical in all their traits. The patterns of variation are complex and are the basis for naming and classifying organisms.

statements.understanding: Species as groups of organisms with shared traits
statements.guidance: This is the original morphological concept of the species as used by Linnaeus.

statements.understanding: Binomial system for naming organisms
statements.guidance: Students should know that the first part of the name identifies the genus, with the second part of the name distinguishing the species. Species in the same genus have similar traits. The genus name is given an initial capital letter but the species name is lowercase.

statements.understanding: Biological species concept
statements.guidance: According to the biological species concept, a species is a group of organisms that can breed and produce fertile offspring. Include possible challenges associated with this definition of a species and that competing species definitions exist.

statements.understanding: Difficulties distinguishing between populations and species due to divergence of non-
statements.guidance: interbreeding populations during speciation Students should understand that speciation is the splitting of one species into two or more. It usually happens gradually rather than by a single act, with populations becoming more and more different in their traits. It can therefore be an arbitrary decision whether two populations are regarded as the same or different species.

statements.understanding: Diversity in chromosome numbers of plant and animal species
statements.guidance: Students should know in general that diversity exists. As an example, students should know that humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees have 48. Students are not required to know other specific chromosome numbers but should appreciate that diploid cells have an even number of chromosomes.

statements.understanding: Karyotyping and karyograms
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should be able to classify chromosomes by banding patterns, length and centromere position. Students should evaluate the evidence for the hypothesis that chromosome 2 in humans arose from the fusion of chromosomes 12 and 13 with a shared primate ancestor. NOS: Students should be able to distinguish between testable hypotheses such as the origin of chromosome 2 and non-testable statements.

statements.understanding: Unity and diversity of genomes within species
statements.guidance: Students should understand that the genome is all the genetic information of an organism. Organisms in the same species share most of their genome but variations such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms give some diversity.

statements.understanding: Diversity of eukaryote genomes
statements.guidance: Genomes vary in overall size, which is determined by the total amount of DNA. Genomes also vary in base sequence. Variation between species is much larger than variation within a species.

statements.understanding: Comparison of genome sizes
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should extract information about genome size for different taxonomic groups from a database to compare genome size to organism complexity.

statements.understanding: Current and potential future uses of whole genome sequencing
statements.guidance: Include the increasing speed and decreasing costs. For current uses, include research into evolutionary relationships and for potential future uses, include personalized medicine.

statements.understanding: Difficulties applying the biological species concept to asexually reproducing species and to
statements.guidance: bacteria that have horizontal gene transfer The biological species concept does not work well with groups of organisms that do not breed sexually or where genes can be transferred from one species to another.

statements.understanding: Chromosome number as a shared trait within a species
statements.guidance: Cross-breeding between closely related species is unlikely to produce fertile offspring if parent chromosome numbers are different.

statements.understanding: Engagement with local plant or animal species to develop a dichotomous key
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should engage with local plant or animal species to develop a dichotomous key.

statements.understanding: Identification of species from environmental DNA in a habitat using barcodes
statements.guidance: Using barcodes and environmental DNA allows the biodiversity of habitats to be investigated rapidly.

statements.understanding: Need for classification of organisms
statements.guidance: Classification is needed because of the immense diversity of species. After classification is completed, a broad range of further study is facilitated.

statements.understanding: Difficulties classifying organisms into the traditional hierarchy of taxa
statements.guidance: The traditional hierarchy of kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species does not always correspond to patterns of divergence generated by evolution. NOS: A fixed ranking of taxa (kingdom, phylum and so on) is arbitrary because it does not reflect the gradation of variation. Cladistics offers an alternative approach to classification using unranked clades. This is an example of the paradigm shift that sometimes occurs in scientific theories.

statements.understanding: Advantages of classification corresponding to evolutionary relationships
statements.guidance: The ideal classification follows evolutionary relationships, so all the members of a taxonomic group have evolved from a common ancestor. Characteristics of organisms within such a group can be predicted because they are shared within a clade.

statements.understanding: Clades as groups of organisms with common ancestry and shared characteristics
statements.guidance: The most objective evidence for placing organisms in the same clade comes from base sequences of genes or amino acid sequences of proteins. Morphological traits can be used to assign organisms to clades.

statements.understanding: Gradual accumulation of sequence differences as the basis for estimates of when clades diverged
statements.guidance: from a common ancestor This method of estimating times is known as the “molecular clock”. The molecular clock can only give estimates because mutation rates are affected by the length of the generation time, the size of a population, the intensity of selective pressure and other factors.

statements.understanding: Base sequences of genes or amino acid sequences of proteins as the basis for constructing
statements.guidance: cladograms Examples can be simple and based on sample data to illustrate the tool. NOS: Students should recognize that different criteria for judgement can lead to different hypotheses. Here, parsimony analysis is used to select the most probable cladogram, in which observed sequence variation between clades is accounted for with the smallest number of sequence changes.

statements.understanding: Analysing cladograms
statements.guidance: Students should be able to deduce evolutionary relationships, common ancestors and clades from a cladogram. They should understand the terms “root”, “node” and “terminal branch” and also that a node represents a hypothetical common ancestor.

statements.understanding: Using cladistics to investigate whether the classification of groups corresponds to evolutionary
statements.guidance: relationships A case study of transfer of plant species between families could be used to develop understanding, for example the reclassification of the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae). However, students are not required to memorize the details of the case study. NOS: Students should appreciate that theories and other scientific knowledge claims may eventually be falsified. In this example, similarities in morphology due to convergent evolution rather than common ancestry suggested a classification that by cladistics has been shown to be false. Note: When students are referring to organisms in an examination, either the common name or the scientific name is acceptable.

statements.understanding: Classification of all organisms into three domains using evidence from rRNA base sequences
statements.guidance: This is the revolutionary reclassification with an extra taxonomic level above kingdoms that was proposed in 1977.

statements.understanding: Evolution as change in the heritable characteristics of a population
statements.guidance: This definition helps to distinguish Darwinian evolution from Lamarckism. Acquired changes that are not genetic in origin are not regarded as evolution. NOS: The theory of evolution by natural selection predicts and explains a broad range of observations and is unlikely ever to be falsified. However, the nature of science makes it impossible to formally prove that it is true by correspondence. It is a pragmatic truth and is therefore referred to as a theory, despite all the supporting evidence.

statements.understanding: Evidence for evolution from base sequences in DNA or RNA and amino acid sequences in proteins
statements.guidance: Sequence data gives powerful evidence of common ancestry.

statements.understanding: Evidence for evolution from selective breeding of domesticated animals and crop plants
statements.guidance: Variation between different domesticated animal breeds and varieties of crop plant, and between them and the original wild species, shows how rapidly evolutionary changes can occur.

statements.understanding: Evidence for evolution from homologous structures
statements.guidance: Include the example of pentadactyl limbs.

statements.understanding: Convergent evolution as the origin of analogous structures
statements.guidance: Students should understand that analogous structures have the same function but different evolutionary origins. Students should know at least one example of analogous features.

statements.understanding: Speciation by splitting of pre-existing species
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that this is the only way in which new species have appeared. Students should also understand that speciation increases the total number of species on Earth, and extinction decreases it. Students should also understand that gradual evolutionary change in a species is not speciation.

statements.understanding: Roles of reproductive isolation and differential selection in speciation
statements.guidance: Include geographical isolation as a means of achieving reproductive isolation. Use the separation of bonobos and common chimpanzees by the Congo River as a specific example of divergence due to differential selection.

statements.understanding: Differences and similarities between sympatric and allopatric speciation
statements.guidance: Students should understand that reproductive isolation can be geographic, behavioural or temporal.

statements.understanding: Adaptive radiation as a source of biodiversity
statements.guidance: Adaptive radiation allows closely related species to coexist without competing, thereby increasing biodiversity in ecosystems where there are vacant niches.

statements.understanding: Barriers to hybridization and sterility of interspecific hybrids as mechanisms for of preventing the
statements.guidance: mixing of alleles between species Courtship behaviour often prevents hybridization in animal species. A mule is an example of a sterile hybrid.

statements.understanding: Abrupt speciation in plants by hybridization and polyploidy
statements.guidance: Use knotweed or smartweed (genus Persicaria) as an example because it contains many species that have been formed by these processes. Note: When students are referring to organisms in an examination, either the common name or the scientific name is acceptable.

statements.understanding: Biodiversity as the variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations
statements.guidance: Include ecosystem diversity, species diversity and genetic diversity.

statements.understanding: Comparisons between current number of species on Earth and past levels of biodiversity
statements.guidance: Millions of species have been discovered, named and described but there are many more species to be discovered. Evidence from fossils suggests that there are currently more species alive on Earth today than at any time in the past. NOS: Classification is an example of pattern recognition but the same observations can be classified in different ways. For example, “splitters” recognize more species than “lumpers” in a taxonomic group.

statements.understanding: Causes of anthropogenic species extinction
statements.guidance: This should be a study of the causes of the current sixth mass extinction, rather than of non-anthropogenic causes of previous mass extinctions. To give a range of causes, carry out three or more brief case studies of species extinction: North Island giant moas (Dinornis novaezealandiae) as an example of the loss of terrestrial megafauna, Caribbean monk seals (Neomonachus tropicalis) as an example of the loss of a marine species, and one other species that has gone extinct from an area that is familiar to students. Note: When students are referring to organisms in an examination, either the common name or the scientific name is acceptable.

statements.understanding: Causes of ecosystem loss
statements.guidance: Students should study only causes that are directly or indirectly anthropogenic. Include two case studies of ecosystem loss. One should be the loss of mixed dipterocarp forest in Southeast Asia, and the other should, if possible, be of a lost ecosystem from an area that is familiar to students.

statements.understanding: Evidence for a biodiversity crisis
statements.guidance: Evidence can be drawn from Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services reports and other sources. Results from reliable surveys of biodiversity in a wide range of habitats around the world are required. Students should understand that surveys need to be repeated to provide evidence of change in species richness and evenness. Note that there are opportunities for contributions from both expert scientists and citizen scientists. NOS: To be verifiable, evidence usually has to come from a published source, which has been peer- reviewed and allows methodology to be checked. Data recorded by citizens rather than scientists brings not only benefits but also unique methodological concerns.

statements.understanding: Causes of the current biodiversity crisis
statements.guidance: Include human population growth as an overarching cause, together with these specific causes: hunting and other forms of over-exploitation; urbanization; deforestation and clearance of land for agriculture with consequent loss of natural habitat; pollution and spread of pests, diseases and invasive alien species due to global transport.

statements.understanding: Need for several approaches to conservation of biodiversity
statements.guidance: No single approach by itself is sufficient, and different species require different measures. Include in situ conservation of species in natural habitats, management of nature reserves, rewilding and reclamation of degraded ecosystems, ex situ conservation in zoos and botanic gardens and storage of germ plasm in seed or tissue banks.

statements.understanding: Selection of evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered species for conservation prioritization
statements.guidance: in the EDGE of Existence programme Students should understand the rationale behind focusing conservation efforts on evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered species (EDGE). NOS: Issues such as which species should be prioritized for conservation efforts have complex ethical, environmental, political, social, cultural and economic implications and therefore need to be debated.

statements.understanding: Chemical properties of a carbon atom allowing for the formation of diverse compounds upon
statements.guidance: which life is based Students should understand the nature of a covalent bond. Students should also understand that a carbon atom can form up to four single bonds or a combination of single and double bonds with other carbon atoms or atoms of other non-metallic elements. Include among the diversity of carbon compounds examples of molecules with branched or unbranched chains and single or multiple rings. NOS: Students should understand that scientific conventions are based on international agreement (SI metric unit prefixes “kilo”, “centi”, “milli”, “micro” and “nano”).

statements.understanding: Production of macromolecules by condensation reactions that link monomers to form a polymer
statements.guidance: Students should be familiar with examples of polysaccharides, polypeptides and nucleic acids.

statements.understanding: Digestion of polymers into monomers by hydrolysis reactions
statements.guidance: Water molecules are split to provide the -H and -OH groups that are incorporated to produce monomers, hence the name of this type of reaction.

statements.understanding: Form and function of monosaccharides
statements.guidance: Students should be able to recognize pentoses and hexoses as monosaccharides from molecular diagrams showing them in the ring forms. Use glucose as an example of the link between the properties of a monosaccharide and how it is used, emphasizing solubility, transportability, chemical stability and the yield of energy from oxidation as properties.

statements.understanding: Polysaccharides as energy storage compounds
statements.guidance: Include the compact nature of starch in plants and glycogen in animals due to coiling and branching during polymerization, the relative insolubility of these compounds due to large molecular size and the relative ease of adding or removing alpha-glucose monomers by condensation and hydrolysis to build or mobilize energy stores.

statements.understanding: Structure of cellulose related to its function as a structural polysaccharide in plants
statements.guidance: Include the alternating orientation of beta-glucose monomers, giving straight chains that can be grouped in bundles and cross-linked with hydrogen bonds.

statements.understanding: Role of glycoproteins in cell–cell recognition
statements.guidance: Include ABO antigens as an example.

statements.understanding: Hydrophobic properties of lipids
statements.guidance: Lipids are substances in living organisms that dissolve in non-polar solvents but are only sparingly soluble in aqueous solvents. Lipids include fats, oils, waxes and steroids.

statements.understanding: Formation of triglycerides and phospholipids by condensation reactions
statements.guidance: One glycerol molecule can link three fatty acid molecules or two fatty acid molecules and one phosphate group.

statements.understanding: Difference between saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids
statements.guidance: Include the number of double carbon (C=C) bonds and how this affects melting point. Relate this to the prevalence of different types of fatty acids in oils and fats used for energy storage in plants and endotherms respectively.

statements.understanding: Triglycerides in adipose tissues for energy storage and thermal insulation
statements.guidance: Students should understand that the properties of triglycerides make them suited to long-term energy storage functions. Students should be able to relate the use of triglycerides as thermal insulators to body temperature and habitat.

statements.understanding: Formation of phospholipid bilayers as a consequence of the hydrophobic and hydrophilic
statements.guidance: regions Students should use and understand the term “amphipathic”.

statements.understanding: Ability of non-polar steroids to pass through the phospholipid bilayer
statements.guidance: Include oestradiol and testosterone as examples. Students should be able to identify compounds as steroids from molecular diagrams.

statements.understanding: Generalized structure of an amino acid
statements.guidance: Students should be able to draw a diagram of a generalized amino acid showing the alpha carbon atom with amine group, carboxyl group, R-group and hydrogen attached.

statements.understanding: Condensation reactions forming dipeptides and longer chains of amino acids
statements.guidance: Students should be able to write the word equation for this reaction and draw a generalized dipeptide after modelling the reaction with molecular models.

statements.understanding: Dietary requirements for amino acids
statements.guidance: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized and must be obtained from food. Non-essential amino acids can be made from other amino acids. Students are not required to give examples of essential and non- essential amino acids. Vegan diets require attention to ensure essential amino acids are consumed.

statements.understanding: Infinite variety of possible peptide chains
statements.guidance: Include the ideas that 20 amino acids are coded for in the genetic code, that peptide chains can have any number of amino acids, from a few to thousands, and that amino acids can be in any order. Students should be familiar with examples of polypeptides.

statements.understanding: Effect of pH and temperature on protein structure
statements.guidance: Include the term “denaturation”.

statements.understanding: Chemical diversity in the R-groups of amino acids as a basis for the immense diversity in protein
statements.guidance: form and function Students are not required to give specific examples of R-groups. However, students should understand that R-groups determine the properties of assembled polypeptides. Students should appreciate that R- groups are hydrophobic or hydrophilic and that hydrophilic R-groups are polar or charged, acidic or basic.

statements.understanding: Impact of primary structure on the conformation of proteins
statements.guidance: Students should understand that the sequence of amino acids and the precise position of each amino acid within a structure determines the three-dimensional shape of proteins. Proteins therefore have precise, predictable and repeatable structures, despite their complexity.

statements.understanding: Pleating and coiling of secondary structure of proteins
statements.guidance: Include hydrogen bonding in regular positions to stabilize alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets.

statements.understanding: Dependence of tertiary structure on hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide covalent bonds and
statements.guidance: hydrophobic interactions Students are not required to name examples of amino acids that participate in these types of bonding, apart from pairs of cysteines forming disulfide bonds. Students should understand that amine and carboxyl groups in R-groups can become positively or negatively charged by binding or dissociation of hydrogen ions and that they can then participate in ionic bonding.

statements.understanding: Effect of polar and non-polar amino acids on tertiary structure of proteins
statements.guidance: In proteins that are soluble in water, hydrophobic amino acids are clustered in the core of globular proteins. Integral proteins have regions with hydrophobic amino acids, helping them to embed in membranes.

statements.understanding: Quaternary structure of non-conjugated and conjugated proteins
statements.guidance: Include insulin and collagen as examples of non-conjugated proteins and haemoglobin as an example of a conjugated protein. NOS: Technology allows imaging of structures that would be impossible to observe with the unaided senses. For example, cryogenic electron microscopy has allowed imaging of single-protein molecules and their interactions with other molecules.

statements.understanding: Relationship of form and function in globular and fibrous proteins
statements.guidance: Students should know the difference in shape between globular and fibrous proteins and understand that their shapes make them suitable for specific functions. Use insulin and collagen to exemplify how form and function are related.

statements.understanding: Lipid bilayers as the basis of cell membranes
statements.guidance: Phospholipids and other amphipathic lipids naturally form continuous sheet-like bilayers in water.

statements.understanding: Lipid bilayers as barriers
statements.guidance: Students should understand that the hydrophobic hydrocarbon chains that form the core of a membrane have low permeability to large molecules and hydrophilic particles, including ions and polar molecules, so membranes function as effective barriers between aqueous solutions.

statements.understanding: Simple diffusion across membranes
statements.guidance: Use movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide molecules between phospholipids as an example of simple diffusion across membranes.

statements.understanding: Integral and peripheral proteins in membranes
statements.guidance: Emphasize that membrane proteins have diverse structures, locations and functions. Integral proteins are embedded in one or both of the lipid layers of a membrane. Peripheral proteins are attached to one or other surface of the bilayer.

statements.understanding: Movement of water molecules across membranes by osmosis and the role of aquaporins
statements.guidance: Include an explanation in terms of random movement of particles, impermeability of membranes to solutes and differences in solute concentration.

statements.understanding: Channel proteins for facilitated diffusion
statements.guidance: Students should understand how the structure of channel proteins makes membranes selectively permeable by allowing specific ions to diffuse through when channels are open but not when they are closed.

statements.understanding: Pump proteins for active transport
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that pumps use energy from adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to transfer specific particles across membranes and therefore that they can move particles against a concentration gradient.

statements.understanding: Selectivity in membrane permeability
statements.guidance: Facilitated diffusion and active transport allow selective permeability in membranes. Permeability by simple diffusion is not selective and depends only on the size and hydrophilic or hydrophobic properties of particles. B.2.1.9—Structure and function of glycoproteins and glycolipids Limit to carbohydrate structures linked to proteins or lipids in membranes, location of carbohydrates on the extracellular side of membranes, and roles in cell adhesion and cell recognition.

statements.understanding: Fluid mosaic model of membrane structure
statements.guidance: Students should be able to draw a two-dimensional representation of the model and include peripheral and integral proteins, glycoproteins, phospholipids and cholesterol. They should also be able to indicate hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions.

statements.understanding: Relationships between fatty acid composition of lipid bilayers and their fluidity
statements.guidance: Unsaturated fatty acids in lipid bilayers have lower melting points, so membranes are fluid and therefore flexible at temperatures experienced by a cell. Saturated fatty acids have higher melting points and make membranes stronger at higher temperatures. Students should be familiar with an example of adaptations in membrane composition in relation to habitat.

statements.understanding: Cholesterol and membrane fluidity in animal cells
statements.guidance: Students should understand the position of cholesterol molecules in membranes and also that cholesterol acts as a modulator (adjustor) of membrane fluidity, stabilizing membranes at higher temperatures and preventing stiffening at lower temperatures.

statements.understanding: Membrane fluidity and the fusion and formation of vesicles
statements.guidance: Include the terms “endocytosis” and “exocytosis”, and examples of each process.

statements.understanding: Gated ion channels in neurons
statements.guidance: Include nicotinic acetylcholine receptors as an example of a neurotransmitter-gated ion channel and sodium and potassium channels as examples of voltage-gated channels.

statements.understanding: Sodium–potassium pumps as an example of exchange transporters
statements.guidance: Include the importance of these pumps in generating membrane potentials.

statements.understanding: Sodium-dependent glucose cotransporters as an example of indirect active transport
statements.guidance: Include the importance of these cotransporters in glucose absorption by cells in the small intestine and glucose reabsorption by cells in the nephron.

statements.understanding: Adhesion of cells to form tissues
statements.guidance: Include the term “cell-adhesion molecules” (CAMs) and the understanding that different forms of CAM are used for different types of cell–cell junction. Students are not required to have detailed knowledge of the different CAMs or junctions.

statements.understanding: Organelles as discrete subunits of cells that are adapted to perform specific functions
statements.guidance: Students should understand that the cell wall, cytoskeleton and cytoplasm are not considered organelles, and that nuclei, vesicles, ribosomes and the plasma membrane are. NOS: Students should recognize that progress in science often follows development of new techniques. For example, study of the function of individual organelles became possible when ultracentrifuges had been invented and methods of using them for cell fractionation had been developed.

statements.understanding: Advantage of the separation of the nucleus and cytoplasm into separate compartments
statements.guidance: Limit to separation of the activities of gene transcription and translation—post-transcriptional modification of mRNA can happen before the mRNA meets ribosomes in the cytoplasm. In prokaryotes this is not possible—mRNA may immediately meet ribosomes.

statements.understanding: Advantages of compartmentalization in the cytoplasm of cells
statements.guidance: Include concentration of metabolites and enzymes and the separation of incompatible biochemical processes. Include lysosomes and phagocytic vacuoles as examples.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of the mitochondrion for production of ATP by aerobic cell respiration
statements.guidance: Include these adaptations: a double membrane with a small volume of intermembrane space, large surface area of cristae and compartmentalization of enzymes and substrates of the Krebs cycle in the matrix.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of the chloroplast for photosynthesis
statements.guidance: Include these adaptations: the large surface area of thylakoid membranes with photosystems, small volumes of fluid inside thylakoids, and compartmentalization of enzymes and substrates of the Calvin cycle in the stroma.

statements.understanding: Functional benefits of the double membrane of the nucleus
statements.guidance: Include the need for pores in the nuclear membrane and for the nucleus membrane to break into vesicles during mitosis and meiosis.

statements.understanding: Structure and function of free ribosomes and of the rough endoplasmic reticulum
statements.guidance: Contrast the synthesis by free ribosomes of proteins for retention in the cell with synthesis by membrane- bound ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum of proteins for transport within the cell and secretion.

statements.understanding: Structure and function of the Golgi apparatus
statements.guidance: Limit to the roles of the Golgi apparatus in processing and secretion of protein.

statements.understanding: Structure and function of vesicles in cells
statements.guidance: Include the role of clathrin in the formation of vesicles.

statements.understanding: Production of unspecialized cells following fertilization and their development into specialized
statements.guidance: cells by differentiation Students should understand the impact of gradients on gene expression within an early-stage embryo.

statements.understanding: Properties of stem cells
statements.guidance: Limit to the capacity of cells to divide endlessly and differentiate along different pathways.

statements.understanding: Location and function of stem cell niches in adult humans
statements.guidance: Limit to two example locations and the understanding that the stem cell niche can maintain the cells or promote their proliferation and differentiation. Bone marrow and hair follicles are suitable examples.

statements.understanding: Differences between totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent stem cells
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that cells in early-stage animal embryos are totipotent but soon become pluripotent, whereas stem cells in adult tissue such as bone marrow are multipotent.

statements.understanding: Cell size as an aspect of specialization
statements.guidance: Consider the range of cell size in humans including male and female gametes, red and white blood cells, neurons and striated muscle fibres.

statements.understanding: Surface area-to-volume ratios and constraints on cell size
statements.guidance: Students should understand the mathematical ratio between volume and surface area and that exchange of materials across a cell surface depends on its area whereas the need for exchange depends on cell volume. NOS: Students should recognize that models are simplified versions of complex systems. In this case, surface-area-to-volume relationship can be modelled using cubes of different side lengths. Although the cubes have a simpler shape than real organisms, scale factors operate in the same way.

statements.understanding: Adaptations to increase surface area-to-volume ratios of cells
statements.guidance: Include flattening of cells, microvilli and invagination. Use erythrocytes and proximal convoluted tubule cells in the nephron as examples.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of type I and type II pneumocytes in alveoli
statements.guidance: Limit to extreme thinness to reduce distances for diffusion in type I pneumocytes and the presence of many secretory vesicles (lamellar bodies) in the cytoplasm that discharge surfactant to the alveolar lumen in type II pneumocytes. Alveolar epithelium is an example of a tissue where more than one cell type is present, because different adaptations are required for the overall function of the tissue.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of cardiac muscle cells and striated muscle fibres
statements.guidance: Include the presence of contractile myofibrils in both muscle types and hypotheses for these differences: branching (branched or unbranched), and length and numbers of nuclei. Also include a discussion of whether a striated muscle fibre is a cell.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of sperm and egg cells
statements.guidance: Limit to gametes in humans.

statements.understanding: Gas exchange as a vital function in all organisms
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that the challenges become greater as organisms increase in size because surface area-to-volume ratio decreases with increasing size, and the distance from the centre of an organism to its exterior increases.

statements.understanding: Properties of gas-exchange surfaces
statements.guidance: Include permeability, thin tissue layer, moisture and large surface area.

statements.understanding: Maintenance of concentration gradients at exchange surfaces in animals
statements.guidance: Include dense networks of blood vessels, continuous blood flow, and ventilation with air for lungs and with water for gills.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of mammalian lungs for gas exchange
statements.guidance: Limit to the alveolar lungs of a mammal. Adaptations should include the presence of surfactant, a branched network of bronchioles, extensive capillary beds and a high surface area.

statements.understanding: Ventilation of the lungs
statements.guidance: Students should understand the role of the diaphragm, intercostal muscles, abdominal muscles and ribs.

statements.understanding: Measurement of lung volumes
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should make measurements to determine tidal volume, vital capacity, and inspiratory and expiratory reserves.

statements.understanding: Adaptations for gas exchange in leaves
statements.guidance: Leaf structure adaptations should include the waxy cuticle, epidermis, air spaces, spongy mesophyll, stomatal guard cells and veins.

statements.understanding: Distribution of tissues in a leaf
statements.guidance: Students should be able to draw and label a plan diagram to show the distribution of tissues in a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf.

statements.understanding: Transpiration as a consequence of gas exchange in a leaf
statements.guidance: Students should be aware of the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.

statements.understanding: Stomatal density
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should use micrographs or perform leaf casts to determine stomatal density. NOS: Reliability of quantitative data is increased by repeating measurements. In this case, repeated counts of the number of stomata visible in the field of view at high power illustrate the variability of biological material and the need for replicate trials.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of foetal and adult haemoglobin for the transport of oxygen
statements.guidance: Include cooperative binding of oxygen to haem groups and allosteric binding of carbon dioxide.

statements.understanding: Bohr shift
statements.guidance: Students should understand how an increase in carbon dioxide causes increased dissociation of oxygen and the benefits of this for actively respiring tissues.

statements.understanding: Oxygen dissociation curves as a means of representing the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen at
statements.guidance: different oxygen concentrations Explain the S-shaped form of the curve in terms of cooperative binding.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of capillaries for exchange of materials between blood and the internal or external
statements.guidance: environment Adaptations should include a large surface area due to branching and narrow diameters, thin walls, and fenestrations in some capillaries where exchange needs to be particularly rapid.

statements.understanding: Structure of arteries and veins
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should be able to distinguish arteries and veins in micrographs from the structure of a vessel wall and its thickness relative to the diameter of the lumen.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of arteries for the transport of blood away from the heart
statements.guidance: Students should understand how the layers of muscle and elastic tissue in the walls of arteries help them to withstand and maintain high blood pressures.

statements.understanding: Measurement of pulse rates
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should be able to determine heart rate by feeling the carotid or radial pulse with fingertips. Traditional methods could be compared with digital ones.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of veins for the return of blood to the heart
statements.guidance: Include valves to prevent backflow and the flexibility of the wall to allow it to be compressed by muscle action.

statements.understanding: Causes and consequences of occlusion of the coronary arteries
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should be able to evaluate epidemiological data relating to the incidence of coronary heart disease. NOS: Students should understand that correlation coefficients quantify correlations between variables and allow the strength of the relationship to be assessed. Low correlation coefficients or lack of any correlation could provide evidence against a hypothesis, but even strong correlations such as that between saturated fat intake and coronary heart disease do not prove a causal link.

statements.understanding: Transport of water from roots to leaves during transpiration
statements.guidance: Students should understand that loss of water by transpiration from cell walls in leaf cells causes water to be drawn out of xylem vessels and through cell walls by capillary action, generating tension (negative pressure potentials). It is this tension that draws water up in the xylem. Cohesion ensures a continuous column of water.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of xylem vessels for transport of water
statements.guidance: Include the lack of cell contents and incomplete or absent end walls for unimpeded flow, lignified walls to withstand tensions, and pits for entry and exit of water.

statements.understanding: Distribution of tissues in a transverse section of the stem of a dicotyledonous plant
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should be able to draw plan diagrams from micrographs to identify the relative positions of vascular bundles, xylem, phloem, cortex and epidermis. Students should annotate the diagram with the main functions of these structures.

statements.understanding: Distribution of tissues in a transverse section of the root of a dicotyledonous plant
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should be able to draw diagrams from micrographs to identify vascular bundles, xylem and phloem, cortex and epidermis.

statements.understanding: Release and reuptake of tissue fluid in capillaries
statements.guidance: Tissue fluid is formed by pressure filtration of plasma in capillaries. This is promoted by the higher pressure of blood from arterioles. Lower pressure in venules allows tissue fluid to drain back into capillaries.

statements.understanding: Exchange of substances between tissue fluid and cells in tissues
statements.guidance: Discuss the composition of plasma and tissue fluid.

statements.understanding: Drainage of excess tissue fluid into lymph ducts
statements.guidance: Limit to the presence of valves and thin walls with gaps in lymph ducts and return of lymph to the blood circulation.

statements.understanding: Differences between the single circulation of bony fish and the double circulation of mammals
statements.guidance: Simple circuit diagrams are sufficient to show the sequence of organs through which blood passes.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of the mammalian heart for delivering pressurized blood to the arteries
statements.guidance: Include form–function adaptations of these structures: cardiac muscle, pacemaker, atria, ventricles, atrioventricular and semilunar valves, septum and coronary vessels. Students should be able to identify these features on a diagram of the heart in the frontal plane and trace the unidirectional flow of blood from named veins to arteries.

statements.understanding: Stages in the cardiac cycle
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should understand the sequence of events in the left side of the heart that follow the initiation of the heartbeat by the sinoatrial node (the “pacemaker”). Students should be able to interpret systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurements from data and graphs.

statements.understanding: Generation of root pressure in xylem vessels by active transport of mineral ions
statements.guidance: Root pressure is positive pressure potential, generated to cause water movement in roots and stems when transport in xylem due to transpiration is insufficient, for example when high humidity prevents transpiration or in spring, before leaves on deciduous plants have opened.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of phloem sieve tubes and companion cells for translocation of sap
statements.guidance: Include sieve plates, reduced cytoplasm and organelles, no nucleus for sieve tube elements and presence of many mitochondria for companion cells and plasmodesmata between them. Students should appreciate how these adaptations ease the flow of sap and enhance loading of carbon compounds into phloem sieve tubes at sources and unloading of them at sinks.

statements.understanding: Adaptations for movement as a universal feature of living organisms
statements.guidance: Students should explore the concept of movement by considering a range of organisms including one motile and one sessile species.

statements.understanding: Sliding filament model of muscle contraction
statements.guidance: Students should understand how a sarcomere contracts by the sliding of actin and myosin filaments.

statements.understanding: Role of the protein titin and antagonistic muscles in muscle relaxation
statements.guidance: The immense protein titin helps sarcomeres to recoil after stretching and also prevents overstretching. Antagonistic muscles are needed because muscle tissue can only exert force when it contracts.

statements.understanding: Structure and function of motor units in skeletal muscle
statements.guidance: Include the motor neuron, muscle fibres and the neuromuscular junctions that connect them.

statements.understanding: Roles of skeletons as anchorage for muscles and as levers
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that arthropods have exoskeletons and vertebrates have endoskeletons.

statements.understanding: Movement at a synovial joint
statements.guidance: Include the roles of bones, cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, muscles and tendons. Use the human hip joint as an example. Students are not required to name muscles and ligaments, but they should be able to name the femur and pelvis.

statements.understanding: Range of motion of a joint
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should compare the range of motion of a joint in a number of dimensions. Students should measure joint angles using computer analysis of images or a goniometer.

statements.understanding: Internal and external intercostal muscles as an example of antagonistic muscle action to facilitate
statements.guidance: internal body movements Students should appreciate that the different orientations of muscle fibres in the internal and external layers of intercostal muscles mean that they move the ribcage in opposite directions and that, when one of these layers contracts, it stretches the other, storing potential energy in the sarcomere protein titin.

statements.understanding: Reasons for locomotion
statements.guidance: Include foraging for food, escaping from danger, searching for a mate and migration, with at least one example of each.

statements.understanding: Adaptations for swimming in marine mammals
statements.guidance: Include streamlining, adaptation of limbs to form flippers and of the tail to form a fluke with up-and-down movement, and changes to the airways to allow periodic breathing between dives.

statements.understanding: Habitat as the place in which a community, species, population or organism lives
statements.guidance: A description of the habitat of a species can include both geographical and physical locations, and the type of ecosystem.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of organisms to the abiotic environment of their habitat
statements.guidance: Include a grass species adapted to sand dunes and a tree species adapted to mangrove swamps.

statements.understanding: Abiotic variables affecting species distribution
statements.guidance: Include examples of abiotic variables for both plants and animals. Students should understand that the adaptations of a species give it a range of tolerance.

statements.understanding: Range of tolerance of a limiting factor
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should use transect data to correlate the distribution of plant or animal species with an abiotic variable. Students should collect this data themselves from a natural or semi- natural habitat. Semi-natural habitats have been influenced by humans but are dominated by wild rather than cultivated species. Sensors could be used to measure abiotic variables such as temperature, light intensity and soil pH.

statements.understanding: Conditions required for coral reef formation
statements.guidance: Coral reefs are used here as an example of a marine ecosystem. Factors should include water depth, pH, salinity, clarity and temperature.

statements.understanding: Abiotic factors as the determinants of terrestrial biome distribution
statements.guidance: Students should understand that, for any given temperature and rainfall pattern, one natural ecosystem type is likely to develop. Illustrate this using a graph showing the distribution of biomes with these two climatic variables on the horizontal and vertical axes.

statements.understanding: Biomes as groups of ecosystems with similar communities due to similar abiotic conditions and
statements.guidance: convergent evolution Students should be familiar with the climate conditions that characterize the tropical forest, temperate forest, taiga, grassland, tundra and hot desert biomes.

statements.understanding: Adaptations to life in hot deserts and tropical rainforest
statements.guidance: Include examples of adaptations in named species of plants and animals.

statements.understanding: Ecological niche as the role of a species in an ecosystem
statements.guidance: Include the biotic and abiotic interactions that influence growth, survival and reproduction, including how a species obtains food.

statements.understanding: Differences between organisms that are obligate anaerobes, facultative anaerobes and obligate
statements.guidance: aerobes Limit to the tolerance of these groups of organisms to the presence or absence of oxygen gas in their environment.

statements.understanding: Photosynthesis as the mode of nutrition in plants, algae and several groups of photosynthetic
statements.guidance: prokaryotes Details of different types of photosynthesis in prokaryotes are not required.

statements.understanding: Holozoic nutrition in animals
statements.guidance: Students should understand that all animals are heterotrophic. In holozoic nutrition food is ingested, digested internally, absorbed and assimilated.

statements.understanding: Mixotrophic nutrition in some protists
statements.guidance: Euglena is a well-known freshwater example of a protist that is both autotrophic and heterotrophic, but many other mixotrophic species are part of oceanic plankton. Students should understand that some mixotrophs are obligate and others are facultative.

statements.understanding: Saprotrophic nutrition in some fungi and bacteria
statements.guidance: Fungi and bacteria with this mode of heterotrophic nutrition can be referred to as decomposers.

statements.understanding: Diversity of nutrition in archaea
statements.guidance: Students should understand that archaea are one of the three domains of life and appreciate that they are metabolically very diverse. Archaea species use either light, oxidation of inorganic chemicals or oxidation of carbon compounds to provide energy for ATP production. Students are not required to name examples.

statements.understanding: Relationship between dentition and the diet of omnivorous and herbivorous representative
statements.guidance: members of the family Hominidae Application of skills: Students should examine models or digital collections of skulls to infer diet from the anatomical features. Examples may include Homo sapiens (humans), Homo floresiensis and Paranthropus robustus. NOS: Deductions can be made from theories. In this example, observation of living mammals led to theories relating dentition to herbivorous or carnivorous diets. These theories allowed the diet of extinct organisms to be deduced.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of herbivores for feeding on plants and of plants for resisting herbivory
statements.guidance: For herbivore adaptations, include piercing and chewing mouthparts of leaf-eating insects. Plants resist herbivory using thorns and other physical structures. Plants also produce toxic secondary compounds in seeds and leaves. Some animals have metabolic adaptations for detoxifying these toxins.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of predators for finding, catching and killing prey and of prey animals for resisting
statements.guidance: predation Students should be aware of chemical, physical and behavioural adaptations in predators and prey.

statements.understanding: Adaptations of plant form for harvesting light
statements.guidance: Include examples from forest ecosystems to illustrate how plants in forests use different strategies to reach light sources, including trees that reach the canopy, lianas, epiphytes growing on branches of trees, strangler epiphytes, shade-tolerant shrubs and herbs growing on the forest floor.

statements.understanding: Fundamental and realized niches
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that fundamental niche is the potential of a species based on adaptations and tolerance limits and that realized niche is the actual extent of a species niche when in competition with other species.

statements.understanding: Competitive exclusion and the uniqueness of ecological niches
statements.guidance: Include elimination of one of the competing species or the restriction of both to a part of their fundamental niche as possible outcomes of competition between two species.

statements.understanding: Enzymes as catalysts
statements.guidance: Students should understand the benefit of increasing rates of reaction in cells.

statements.understanding: Role of enzymes in metabolism
statements.guidance: Students should understand that metabolism is the complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions occurring in living organisms. Because of enzyme specificity, many different enzymes are required by living organisms, and control over metabolism can be exerted through these enzymes.

statements.understanding: Anabolic and catabolic reactions
statements.guidance: Examples of anabolism should include the formation of macromolecules from monomers by condensation reactions including protein synthesis, glycogen formation and photosynthesis. Examples of catabolism should include hydrolysis of macromolecules into monomers in digestion and oxidation of substrates in respiration.

statements.understanding: Enzymes as globular proteins with an active site for catalysis
statements.guidance: Include that the active site is composed of a few amino acids only, but interactions between amino acids within the overall three-dimensional structure of the enzyme ensure that the active site has the necessary properties for catalysis.

statements.understanding: Interactions between substrate and active site to allow induced-fit binding
statements.guidance: Students should recognize that both substrate and enzymes change shape when binding occurs.

statements.understanding: Role of molecular motion and substrate-active site collisions in enzyme catalysis
statements.guidance: Movement is needed for a substrate molecule and an active site to come together. Sometimes large substrate molecules are immobilized while sometimes enzymes can be immobilized by being embedded in membranes.

statements.understanding: Relationships between the structure of the active site, enzyme–substrate specificity and
statements.guidance: denaturation Students should be able to explain these relationships.

statements.understanding: Effects of temperature, pH and substrate concentration on the rate of enzyme activity
statements.guidance: The effects should be explained with reference to collision theory and denaturation. Application of skills: Students should be able to interpret graphs showing the effects. NOS: Students should be able to describe the relationship between variables as shown in graphs. They should recognize that generalized sketches of relationships are examples of models in biology. Models in the form of sketch graphs can be evaluated using results from enzyme experiments.

statements.understanding: Measurements in enzyme-catalysed reactions
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should determine reaction rates through experimentation and using secondary data.

statements.understanding: Effect of enzymes on activation energy
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should appreciate that energy is required to break bonds within the substrate and that there is an energy yield when bonds are made to form the products of an enzyme- catalysed reaction. Students should be able to interpret graphs showing this effect.

statements.understanding: Intracellular and extracellular enzyme-catalysed reactions
statements.guidance: Include glycolysis and the Krebs cycle as intracellular examples and chemical digestion in the gut as an extracellular example.

statements.understanding: Generation of heat energy by the reactions of metabolism
statements.guidance: Include the idea that heat generation is inevitable because metabolic reactions are not 100% efficient in energy transfer. Mammals, birds and some other animals depend on this heat production for maintenance of constant body temperature.

statements.understanding: Cyclical and linear pathways in metabolism
statements.guidance: Use glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the Calvin cycle as examples.

statements.understanding: Allosteric sites and non-competitive inhibition
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that only specific substances can bind to an allosteric site. Binding causes interactions within an enzyme that lead to conformational changes, which alter the active site enough to prevent catalysis. Binding is reversible.

statements.understanding: Competitive inhibition as a consequence of an inhibitor binding reversibly to an active site
statements.guidance: Use statins as an example of competitive inhibitors. Include the difference between competitive and non- competitive inhibition in the interactions between substrate and inhibitor and therefore in the effect of substrate concentration.

statements.understanding: Regulation of metabolic pathways by feedback inhibition
statements.guidance: Use the pathway that produces isoleucine as an example of an end product acting as an inhibitor.

statements.understanding: Mechanism-based inhibition as a consequence of chemical changes to the active site caused by
statements.guidance: the irreversible binding of an inhibitor Use penicillin as an example. Include the change to transpeptidases that confers resistance to penicillin.

statements.understanding: ATP as the molecule that distributes energy within cells
statements.guidance: Include the full name of ATP (adenosine triphosphate) and that it is a nucleotide. Students should appreciate the properties of ATP that make it suitable for use as the energy currency within cells.

statements.understanding: Life processes within cells that ATP supplies with energy
statements.guidance: Include active transport across membranes, synthesis of macromolecules (anabolism), movement of the whole cell or cell components such as chromosomes.

statements.understanding: Energy transfers during interconversions between ATP and ADP
statements.guidance: Students should know that energy is released by hydrolysis of ATP (adenosine triphosphate) to ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and phosphate, but energy is required to synthesize ATP from ADP and phosphate. Students are not required to know the quantity of energy in kilojoules, but students should appreciate that it is sufficient for many tasks in the cell.

statements.understanding: Cell respiration as a system for producing ATP within the cell using energy released from carbon
statements.guidance: compounds Students should appreciate that glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates for cell respiration but that a wide range of carbon/organic compounds can be used. Students should be able to distinguish between the processes of cell respiration and gas exchange.

statements.understanding: Differences between anaerobic and aerobic cell respiration in humans
statements.guidance: Include which respiratory substrates can be used, whether oxygen is required, relative yields of ATP, types of waste product and where the reactions occur in a cell. Students should be able to write simple word equations for both types of respiration, with glucose as the substrate. Students should appreciate that mitochondria are required for aerobic, but not anaerobic, respiration.

statements.understanding: Variables affecting the rate of cell respiration
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should make measurements allowing for the determination of the rate of cell respiration. Students should also be able to calculate the rate of cellular respiration from raw data that they have generated experimentally or from secondary data.

statements.understanding: Role of NAD as a carrier of hydrogen and oxidation by removal of hydrogen during cell respiration
statements.guidance: Students should understand that oxidation is a process of electron loss, so when hydrogen with an electron is removed from a substrate (dehydrogenation) the substrate has been oxidized. They should appreciate that redox reactions involve both oxidation and reduction, and that NAD is reduced when it accepts hydrogen.

statements.understanding: Conversion of glucose to pyruvate by stepwise reactions in glycolysis with a net yield of ATP and
statements.guidance: reduced NAD Include phosphorylation, lysis, oxidation and ATP formation. Students are not required to know the names of the intermediates, but students should know that each step in the pathway is catalysed by a different enzyme.

statements.understanding: Conversion of pyruvate to lactate as a means of regenerating NAD in anaerobic cell respiration
statements.guidance: Regeneration of NAD allows glycolysis to continue, with a net yield of two ATP molecules per molecule of glucose.

statements.understanding: Anaerobic cell respiration in yeast and its use in brewing and baking
statements.guidance: Students should understand that the pathways of anaerobic respiration are the same in humans and yeasts apart from the regeneration of NAD using pyruvate and therefore the final products.
