statements.guidance: Show alleles carried on X chromosomes as superscript letters on an uppercase X.

statements.understanding: Pedigree charts to deduce patterns of inheritance of genetic disorders
statements.guidance: Students should understand the genetic basis for the prohibition of marriage between close relatives in many societies. NOS: Scientists draw general conclusions by inductive reasoning when they base a theory on observations of some but not all cases. A pattern of inheritance may be deduced from parts of a pedigree chart and this theory may then allow genotypes of specific individuals in the pedigree to be deduced. Students should be able to distinguish between inductive and deductive reasoning.

statements.understanding: Continuous variation due to polygenic inheritance and/or environmental factors
statements.guidance: Use skin colour in humans as an example. Application of skills: Students should understand the distinction between continuous variables such as skin colour and discrete variables such as ABO blood group. They should also be able to apply measures of central tendency such as mean, median and mode.

statements.understanding: Box-and-whisker plots to represent data for a continuous variable such as student height
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should use a box-and-whisker plot to display six aspects of data: outliers, minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile and maximum. A data point is categorized as an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR (interquartile range) above the third quartile or below the first quartile.

statements.understanding: Segregation and independent assortment of unlinked genes in meiosis
statements.guidance: Students should understand the link between the movements of chromosomes in meiosis and the outcome of dihybrid crosses involving pairs of unlinked genes.

statements.understanding: Punnett grids for predicting genotypic and phenotypic ratios in dihybrid crosses involving pairs
statements.guidance: of unlinked autosomal genes Students should understand how the 9:3:3:1 and 1:1:1:1 ratios are derived. NOS: 9:3:3:1 and 1:1:1:1 ratios for dihybrid crosses are based on what has been called Mendel’s second law. This law only applies if genes are on different chromosomes or are far apart enough on one chromosome for recombination rates to reach 50%. Students should recognize that there are exceptions to all biological “laws” under certain conditions.

statements.understanding: Loci of human genes and their polypeptide products
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should explore genes and their polypeptide products in databases. They should find pairs of genes with loci on different chromosomes and also in close proximity on the same chromosome.

statements.understanding: Autosomal gene linkage
statements.guidance: In crosses involving linkage, the symbols used to denote alleles should be shown alongside vertical lines representing homologous chromosomes. Students should understand the reason that alleles of linked genes can fail to assort independently.

statements.understanding: Recombinants in crosses involving two linked or unlinked genes
statements.guidance: Students should understand how to determine the outcomes of crosses between an individual heterozygous for both genes and an individual homozygous recessive for both genes. Identify recombinants in gametes, in genotypes of offspring and in phenotypes of offspring.

statements.understanding: Use of a chi-squared test on data from dihybrid crosses
statements.guidance: Students should understand the concept of statistical significance, the p = 0.05 level, null/alternative hypothesis and the idea of observed versus expected results. NOS: Students should recognize that statistical testing often involves using a sample to represent a population. In this case the sample is the F2 generation. In many experiments the sample is the replicated or repeated measurements.

statements.understanding: Homeostasis as maintenance of the internal environment of an organism
statements.guidance: Variables are kept within preset limits, despite fluctuations in external environment. Include body temperature, blood pH, blood glucose concentration and blood osmotic concentration as homeostatic variables in humans.

statements.understanding: Negative feedback loops in homeostasis
statements.guidance: Students should understand the reason for use of negative rather than positive feedback control in homeostasis and also that negative feedback returns homeostatic variables to the set point from values above and below the set point.

statements.understanding: Regulation of blood glucose as an example of the role of hormones in homeostasis
statements.guidance: Include control of secretion of insulin and glucagon by pancreatic endocrine cells, transport in blood and the effects on target cells.

statements.understanding: Physiological changes that form the basis of type 1 and type 2 diabetes
statements.guidance: Students should understand the physiological changes, together with risk factors and methods of prevention and treatment.

statements.understanding: Thermoregulation as an example of negative feedback control
statements.guidance: Include the roles of peripheral thermoreceptors, the hypothalamus and pituitary gland, thyroxin and also examples of muscle and adipose tissue that act as effectors of temperature change.

statements.understanding: Thermoregulation mechanisms in humans
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that birds and mammals regulate their body temperature by physiological and behavioural means. Students are only required to understand the details of thermoregulation for humans. Include vasodilation, vasoconstriction, shivering, sweating, uncoupled respiration in brown adipose tissue and hair erection.

statements.understanding: Role of the kidney in osmoregulation and excretion
statements.guidance: Students should understand the distinction between excretion and osmoregulation. Osmoregulation is regulation of osmotic concentration. The units for osmotic concentration are osmoles per litre (osmol L−1).

statements.understanding: Role of the glomerulus, Bowman’s capsule and proximal convoluted tubule in excretion
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate how ultrafiltration remove solutes from blood plasma and how useful substances are then reabsorbed, to leave toxins and other unwanted solutes in the filtrate, which are excreted in urine.

statements.understanding: Role of the loop of Henle
statements.guidance: Limit to active transport of sodium ions in the ascending limb to maintain high osmotic concentrations in the medulla, facilitating water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.

statements.understanding: Osmoregulation by water reabsorption in the collecting ducts
statements.guidance: Include the roles of osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, changes to the rate of antidiuretic hormone secretion by the pituitary gland and the resultant switches in location of aquaporins between cell membranes and intracellular vesicles in cells of the collecting ducts.

statements.understanding: Changes in blood supply to organs in response to changes in activity
statements.guidance: As examples, use the pattern of blood supply to the skeletal muscles, gut, brain and kidneys during sleep, vigorous physical activity and wakeful rest.

statements.understanding: Natural selection as the mechanism driving evolutionary change
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that natural selection operates continuously and over billions of years, resulting in the biodiversity of life on Earth. NOS: In Darwin’s time it was widely understood that species evolved, but the mechanism was not clear. Darwin’s theory provided a convincing mechanism and replaced Lamarckism. This is an example of a paradigm shift. Students should understand the meaning of the term “paradigm shift”.

statements.understanding: Roles of mutation and sexual reproduction in generating the variation on which natural selection
statements.guidance: acts Mutation generates new alleles and sexual reproduction generates new combinations of alleles.

statements.understanding: Overproduction of offspring and competition for resources as factors that promote natural
statements.guidance: selection Include examples of food and other resources that may limit carrying capacity.

statements.understanding: Abiotic factors as selection pressures
statements.guidance: Include examples of density-independent factors such as high or low temperatures that may affect survival of individuals in a population.

statements.understanding: Differences between individuals in adaptation, survival and reproduction as the basis for natural
statements.guidance: selection Students are required to study natural selection due to intraspecific competition, including the concept of fitness when discussing the survival value and reproductive potential of a genotype.

statements.understanding: Requirement that traits are heritable for evolutionary change to occur
statements.guidance: Students should understand that characteristics acquired during an individual’s life due to environmental factors are not encoded in the base sequence of genes and so are not heritable.

statements.understanding: Sexual selection as a selection pressure in animal species
statements.guidance: Differences in physical and behavioural traits, which can be used as signs of overall fitness, can affect success in attracting a mate and so drive the evolution of an animal population. Illustrate this using suitable examples such as the evolution of the plumage of birds of paradise.

statements.understanding: Modelling of sexual and natural selection based on experimental control of selection pressures
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should interpret data from John Endler’s experiments with guppies.

statements.understanding: Concept of the gene pool
statements.guidance: A gene pool consists of all the genes and their different alleles, present in a population.

statements.understanding: Allele frequencies of geographically isolated populations
statements.guidance: Application of skills: Students should use databases to search allele frequencies. Use at least one human example.

statements.understanding: Changes in allele frequency in the gene pool as a consequence of natural selection between
statements.guidance: individuals according to differences in their heritable traits Darwin developed the theory of evolution by natural selection. Biologists subsequently integrated genetics with natural selection in what is now known as neo-Darwinism.

statements.understanding: Differences between directional, disruptive and stabilizing selection
statements.guidance: Students should be aware that all three types result in a change in allele frequency.

statements.understanding: Hardy–Weinberg equation and calculations of allele or genotype frequencies
statements.guidance: Use p and q to denote the two allele frequencies. Students should understand that p + q = 1 so genotype frequencies are predicted by the Hardy–Weinberg equation: p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1. If one of the genotype frequencies is known, the allele frequencies can be calculated using the same equations.

statements.understanding: Hardy–Weinberg conditions that must be maintained for a population to be in genetic
statements.guidance: equilibrium Students should understand that if genotype frequencies in a population do not fit the Hardy–Weinberg equation, this indicates that one or more of the conditions is not being met, for example mating is non- random or survival rates vary between genotypes.

statements.understanding: Artificial selection by deliberate choice of traits
statements.guidance: Artificial selection is carried out in crop plants and domesticated animals by choosing individuals for breeding that have desirable traits. Unintended consequences of human actions, such as the evolution of resistance in bacteria when an antibiotic is used, are due to natural rather than artificial selection.

statements.understanding: Stability as a property of natural ecosystems
statements.guidance: Illustrate ecosystem stability with evidence of forest, desert or other ecosystems that have shown continuity over long periods. There is evidence for some ecosystems persisting for millions of years.

statements.understanding: Requirements for stability in ecosystems
statements.guidance: Include supply of energy, recycling of nutrients, genetic diversity and climatic variables remaining within tolerance levels.

statements.understanding: Deforestation of Amazon rainforest as an example of a possible tipping point in ecosystem
statements.guidance: stability Include the need for a large area of rainforest for the generation of atmospheric water vapour by transpiration, with consequent cooling, air flows and rainfall. Include uncertainty over the minimum area of rainforest that is sufficient to maintain these processes. Application of skills: Students should be able to calculate percentage change. In this case the extent of deforestation can be assessed by calculating the percentage change from the original area of forest.

statements.understanding: Use of a model to investigate the effect of variables on ecosystem stability
statements.guidance: Mesocosms can be set up in open tanks but sealed glass vessels are preferable because entry and exit of matter can be prevented but energy transfer is still possible. Aquatic or microbial ecosystems are likely to be more successful than terrestrial ones. NOS: Care and maintenance of the mesocosms should follow IB experimental guidelines.

statements.understanding: Role of keystone species in the stability of ecosystems
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate the disproportionate impact on community structure of keystone species and the risk of ecosystem collapse if they are removed.

statements.understanding: Assessing sustainability of resource harvesting from natural ecosystems
statements.guidance: Sustainability depends on the rate of harvesting being lower than the rate of replacement. Include one terrestrial plant species and one species of marine fish as examples of renewable resources and how sustainability of harvesting can be assessed.

statements.understanding: Factors affecting the sustainability of agriculture
statements.guidance: Include the need to consider soil erosion, leaching of nutrients, supply of fertilizers and other inputs, pollution due to agrochemicals, and carbon footprint.

statements.understanding: Eutrophication of aquatic and marine ecosystems due to leaching
statements.guidance: Students should understand the effects of eutrophication resulting from leaching of nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers, including increased biochemical oxygen demand (BOD).

statements.understanding: Biomagnification of pollutants in natural ecosystems
statements.guidance: Students should understand how increased levels of toxins accumulate in the tissues of consumers in higher trophic levels. Include DDT and mercury as examples.

statements.understanding: Effects of microplastic and macroplastic pollution of the oceans
statements.guidance: Students should understand that plastics are persistent in the natural environment due to non- biodegradability. Include examples of the effects of plastic pollution on marine life. NOS: Scientists can influence the actions of citizens if they provide clear information about their research findings. Popular media coverage of the effects of plastic pollution on marine life changed public perception globally, which has driven measures to address this problem.

statements.understanding: Restoration of natural processes in ecosystems by rewilding
statements.guidance: Methods should include reintroduction of apex predators and other keystone species, re-establishment of connectivity of habitats over large areas, and minimization of human impact including by ecological management. Include the example of Hinewai Reserve in New Zealand.

statements.understanding: Ecological succession and its causes
statements.guidance: Succession can be triggered by changes in both an abiotic environment and in biotic factors.

statements.understanding: Changes occurring during primary succession
statements.guidance: Use any suitable terrestrial example to illustrate these general principles: increases in size of plants, amount of primary production, species diversity, complexity of food webs and amount of nutrient cycling.

statements.understanding: Cyclical succession in ecosystems
statements.guidance: Students should appreciate that in some ecosystems there is a cycle of communities rather than a single unchanging climax community. Students should refer to an example.

statements.understanding: Climax communities and arrested succession
statements.guidance: Given any specific environmental conditions, ecological succession tends to lead to a particular type of climax community, but human influences can prevent this from developing. Use grazing by farm livestock and drainage of wetlands as examples.

statements.understanding: Anthropogenic causes of climate change
statements.guidance: Limit to anthropogenic increases in atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane. NOS: Students should be able to distinguish between positive and negative correlation and should also distinguish between correlation and causation. For example, data from Antarctic ice cores shows a positive correlation between global temperatures and atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations over hundreds of thousands of years. This correlation does not prove that carbon dioxide in the atmosphere increases global temperatures, although other evidence confirms the causal link.

statements.understanding: Positive feedback cycles in global warming
statements.guidance: Include release of carbon dioxide from deep ocean, increases in absorption of solar radiation due to loss of reflective snow and ice, accelerating rates of decomposition of peat and previously undecomposed organic matter in permafrost, release of methane from melting permafrost and increases in droughts and forest fires.

statements.understanding: Change from net carbon accumulation to net loss in boreal forests as an example of a tipping
statements.guidance: point Include warmer temperatures and decreased winter snowfall leading to increased incidence of drought and reductions in primary production in taiga, with forest browning and increases in the frequency and intensity of forest fires, which result in legacy carbon combustion.

statements.understanding: Melting of landfast ice and sea ice as examples of polar habitat change
statements.guidance: Include potential loss of breeding grounds of the emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) due to early breakout of landfast ice in the Antarctic and loss of sea ice habitat for walruses in the Arctic. Note: When students are referring to organisms in an examination, either the common name or the scientific name is acceptable.

statements.understanding: Changes in ocean currents altering the timing and extent of nutrient upwelling
statements.guidance: Warmer surface water can prevent nutrient upwelling to the surface, decreasing ocean primary production and energy flow through marine food chains.

statements.understanding: Poleward and upslope range shifts of temperate species
statements.guidance: As evidence-based examples, include upslope range shifts for tropical-zone montane bird species in New Guinea and range contraction and northward spread in North American tree species.

statements.understanding: Threats to coral reefs as an example of potential ecosystem collapse
statements.guidance: Increased carbon dioxide concentrations are the cause of ocean acidification and suppression of calcification in corals. Increases in water temperature are a cause of coral bleaching. Loss of corals causes the collapse of reef ecosystems.

statements.understanding: Afforestation, forest regeneration and restoration of peat-forming wetlands as approaches to
statements.guidance: carbon sequestration NOS: There is active scientific debate over whether plantations of non-native tree species or rewilding with native species offer the best approach to carbon sequestration. Peat formation naturally occurs in waterlogged soils in temperate and boreal zones and also very rapidly in some tropical ecosystems.

statements.understanding: Phenology as research into the timing of biological events
statements.guidance: Students should be aware that photoperiod and temperature patterns are examples of variables that influence the timing of biological events such as flowering, budburst and bud set in deciduous trees, bird migration and nesting.

statements.understanding: Disruption to the synchrony of phenological events by climate change
statements.guidance: Students should recognize that within an ecosystem temperature may act as the cue in one population and photoperiod may be the cue in another. Include spring growth of the Arctic mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium arcticum) and arrival of migrating reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) as one example. Also include a suitable local example or use the breeding of the great tit (Parus major) and peak biomass of caterpillars in north European forests as another. Note: When students are referring to organisms in an examination, either the common name or the scientific name is acceptable.

statements.understanding: Increases to the number of insect life cycles within a year due to climate change
statements.guidance: Use the spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus or Dendroctonus micans) as an example. Note: When students are referring to organisms in an examination, either the common name or the scientific name is acceptable.

statements.understanding: Evolution as a consequence of climate change
statements.guidance: Include changes in the fitness of colour variants of the tawny owl (Strix aluco) as a consequence of changes in snow cover. Note: When students are referring to organisms in an examination, either the common name or the scientific name is acceptable.
